description: Created in 1945 to prevent war, the **UN** saves millions of lives every year, while remaining paralyzed in the face of the greatest conflicts.

hero.hook: Five countries alone can block any decision by the organization supposed to maintain world peace.

blocks.text: The **UN**, the United Nations, was born from the ashes of the Second World War with an immense ambition: to replace force with law. Founded in 1945, it succeeds a League of Nations which failed to prevent the Second World War.

However, from the Cold War to current tensions, the institution often seems powerless in the face of great powers. Between indisputable humanitarian successes and repeated political paralysis, the UN resembles a colossus with feet of clay.

The architecture of the UN is not the fruit of a global democracy, but of a compromise between the victors of 1945. Its most powerful body, the **[[Security Council]]**, has fifteen members, but only five of them hold the reality of power: the United States, Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom.
The UN headquarters in New York is an international territory. Billionaire John D. Rockefeller Jr. offered $8.5 million to buy the land, previously occupied by slaughterhouses.

These five powers have a right of veto which allows a single state to block any decision, even supported by the immense majority of other countries. This mechanism was to prevent the great powers from going to war with each other. It has become the instrument of almost systematic paralysis: the Russian veto blocks all action in Ukraine, the American veto protects its allies in the Middle East.

If the political UN is often blocked, the operational UN records real victories. This success is based on the **[[UN specialized agencies]]**, which has its own budgets and expert personnel acting far from the diplomatic jousts of New York.

One of the greatest successes in human history, the eradication of smallpox in 1980, was coordinated by the World Health Organization. The World Food Program feeds nearly 100 million people affected by famine each year.

blocks.caption: UN peacekeepers intervene to stabilize regions after a ceasefire.

blocks.text: In terms of security, the Blue Helmets embody the visible face of UN action. Their mission is not to wage war, but to intervene between belligerents after a ceasefire. Criticized after tragic failures in Rwanda or Bosnia, they remain essential to stabilize certain areas and allow the deployment of humanitarian aid.

sections.title: The effectiveness of the shadows: the humanitarian arm

blocks.text: The fundamental limitation of the UN lies in the principle of national sovereignty: it cannot intervene in the internal affairs of a State. This principle protects against arbitrary interference, but it also sometimes serves as a shield for dictatorships.

To fill this gap, a new concept appeared in 2005: the . According to this principle, if a state fails to protect its population against mass crimes, the international community has a duty to intervene. But its implementation still requires the agreement of the Security Council, which strongly limits its scope. **[[The Responsibility to Protect (R2P)]]**
It was American President Franklin D. Roosevelt who invented the name “United Nations” in 1942, proposing it to Winston Churchill while the latter was in the bath.

The **[[General Assembly]]**, where each country has one vote, remains the only truly universal place for debate. Its resolutions are not binding, but they form a powerful barometer of world opinion that even great powers cannot completely ignore.

The debate over UN reform is as old as the institution itself. Almost all diplomats recognize the outdated nature of the current Security Council: the absence of India, Japan or any African nation among the permanent members undermines its legitimacy in the eyes of much of the world.

But modifying the United Nations Charter requires ratification by two-thirds of the member states, necessarily including the five permanent members. None of these powers is ready to give up or even limit their veto power.
The veto power of the five permanent members of the Security Council has been used more than 300 times since 1945, regularly blocking any action in conflicts that directly involve the great powers.
